Start working on Linear ticket eng-2363 by fetching its details and creating a dedicated git worktree.

## Steps

### 1. Validate input
- `eng-2363` should be a Linear ticket ID like `ENG-1271`. If missing or malformed, ask the user.

### 2. Fetch ticket details from Linear
- Use `mcp__linear-server__get_issue` with the issue ID `eng-2363`
- Extract: title, description, and `branchName` (Linear provides this)
- If the Linear tool is unavailable, ask the user for a branch name manually

### 3. Determine branch name
- Use the `branchName` field from Linear if available (it's already formatted correctly)
- Otherwise derive it: lowercase the ticket ID + hyphenated slug of the title
  - Example: `ENG-1271 Implement filter search` → `eng-1271-implement-filter-search`
  - Strip special characters, replace spaces with hyphens, truncate to ~60 chars

### 4. Create git worktree
Run these from the repo root (the main working directory, not an existing worktree):

```bash
# Fetch latest main so the worktree starts from up-to-date origin/main
git fetch origin main

# Check if branch already exists
git branch --list <branch-name>

# Check if worktree already exists
git worktree list | grep <branch-name>
```

- **If worktree already exists**: skip to step 5, just `cd` into `.claude/worktrees/<branch-name>`
- **If branch does NOT exist**: `git worktree add -b <branch-name> .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> origin/main`
- **If branch already exists but no worktree**: reset the branch to `origin/main` first, then add the worktree:
  ```bash
  git branch -f <branch-name> origin/main
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> <branch-name>
  ```

### 5. Enter the worktree
**Do NOT use the `EnterWorktree` tool** — it always creates a brand-new worktree and will duplicate the one you just created.

Instead, use `cd` to switch into the worktree directory:
```bash
cd .claude/worktrees/<branch-name>
```

All subsequent commands should run from this path.

### 6. Install dependencies and set up the worktree
After entering the worktree, run the following to bootstrap the environment:

```bash
pnpm install
```

This is required because worktrees share git objects but each needs its own `node_modules`.

### 6b. Copy .env files from the main repo into the worktree
`.env` files are gitignored, so each worktree needs its own copies. After `pnpm install`, copy all `.env` files (excluding `.env.example` files) from the main repo root into the matching relative paths in the worktree.

The main repo root is the working directory you were in before entering the worktree (e.g. `/Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph`).

Run:
```bash
# From the main repo root, find all .env files (not .env.example) and copy them into the worktree
find . -name ".env*" \
  -not -name ".env.example" \
  -not -path "./.git/*" \
  -not -path "./node_modules/*" \
  -not -path "./.claude/worktrees/*" \
  | while read f; do
      dest=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>/$f"
      mkdir -p "$(dirname "$dest")"
      cp "$f" "$dest"
    done
```

Report which files were copied so the user can confirm.

The copied `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` points at the main checkout's vault. Step 7 replaces it
with the vault leased to this worktree.

### 6c. Link the shared `dg-*` skills into the worktree

Claude Code only loads skills from `.claude/skills`, but the repo's shared skills live in
`.agents/skills`. Without this step they never load in the worktree: they cannot trigger on
their own descriptions and have no slash command.

Run from the main repo root, substituting the worktree path:

```bash
WT=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>"
MAIN="$PWD"
mkdir -p "$WT/.claude/skills"
for src in "$MAIN"/.agents/skills/dg-*/; do
  s=$(basename "$src")
  if [ -d "$WT/.agents/skills/$s" ]; then
    # Relative link, so the worktree uses its own branch's copy of the skill.
    ln -sfn "../../.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  else
    # Branch predates the skill; fall back to the main checkout's copy.
    ln -sfn "$MAIN/.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  fi
done
ls -l "$WT/.claude/skills/"
```

Verify each link resolves before moving on:

```bash
for d in "$WT"/.claude/skills/dg-*; do
  [ -f "$d/SKILL.md" ] || echo "BROKEN: $d"
done
```

These links are gitignored (`.claude/*`), so they are local to this machine and add nothing
to the diff. Use a glob rather than a variable list: zsh does not word-split unquoted
variables, so `for s in $SKILLS` silently iterates once with the whole string.

### 7. Ask the user which app to start
Ask the user which app they want to run in dev mode. Common options:
- **Roam**: `SUPABASE_USE_DB=none pnpm -C <worktree>/apps/roam dev`
- **Obsidian**: `node ~/.claude/skills/obsidian-vault/scripts/vault.mjs dev --worktree <worktree>`
  - This leases a free local-db vault and writes `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` and `SUPABASE_USE_DB` for
    it into `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It then starts the watcher. A later plain `pnpm dev`
    and CDP runs use the same vault. Add `--db production` only if the user asks to test against
    prod (testVault123).
  - For **None**, still run `vault.mjs claim --worktree <worktree>` if the ticket touches
    apps/obsidian, so the `.env` doesn't keep pointing at the main checkout's vault.
  - **Exit 2** means every vault in that pool is taken. Follow the `obsidian-vault` skill: ask the
    user which vault to take over, then rerun with `--take <vault>`. Never pick one yourself.
  - On success, pass the printed `obsidian://open?path=` URL to the user, so they open that vault.
- **None**: just set up the environment without starting a dev server

If the user says Roam, also switch the Roam dev symlink:
```bash
ln -sfn <worktree>/apps/roam/dist ~/roam-ext-dev
```
and remind them to reload the developer extension in Roam.

Run the chosen dev command in the background so the user can continue working.

**Dev server gotchas** (learned the hard way — don't rediscover these):

- The filter flag is `--filter`, not `--F`. Turbo 2.5.6 rejects `--F=roam` outright.
- Prefer `pnpm -C <abs-path> <app> dev` over `turbo dev --filter=<app>`. `turbo dev --filter=roam`
  also runs the `@repo/database#dev` dependency, which requires Docker Desktop plus an explicit
  `SUPABASE_USE_DB`; if Docker isn't running turbo fails the *entire* run even though the app
  itself built fine. Going through `pnpm -C` skips the dependency graph.
- `SUPABASE_USE_DB` must be one of `local | branch | production | none | implicit`
  (see `packages/database/src/dbDotEnv.mjs`). Use `none` for work that doesn't touch the database.
- **Always bake the absolute worktree path into the command.** The Bash tool's cwd resets to the
  main repo between calls, so a backgrounded `pnpm --filter roam dev` with no path silently builds
  the *main repo's* `dist` — not the worktree the symlink points at. `pnpm -C <abs-path>` makes the
  path intrinsic to the command so it can't be dropped.
- After starting, verify before reporting success: confirm the log says `built with 0 errors` **and**
  that `<worktree>/apps/roam/dist` has a fresh mtime. A background task that failed still returns a
  task ID.

### 8. Ingest any saved session context
The branch may have been worked on before (e.g. reset from an existing branch).
Check for recorded session context:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, **read the `CONTEXT_FILE`** and load it as working context
  (`Next step`, `Open questions`, `Key decisions`, `Dead ends`).
- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=no` or the command errors, continue — this is a fresh start.

### 9. Show context
After setup, display:
- Ticket ID and title
- Branch name you're on
- Brief description from the ticket (if available)
- Which app dev server is running (if any), and for Obsidian, which vault is leased
- That the shared `dg-*` skills are linked and resolving
- If prior session context was found: its `TL;DR` and `Next step`
- A short "ready to work" confirmation
- Remind the user they can run `/checkpoint` to save session context before wrapping up

content.text:
# Plan: Obsidian docs page for schema import and export (ENG-2363)

Nothing here needs code changes. The feature is Obsidian-only (Roam has no equivalent), and no existing docs page mentions it.

## Where the page goes

- **New page:** `apps/website/content/obsidian/configuration/schema-import-export.mdx`, listed in `configuration/_meta.ts` right after `relationship-types`. The sidebar label would be "Import and export schema".
- **Why configuration:** a schema is node types, relation types and templates, and those pages already live in this section. The feature doesn't depend on sync, so it doesn't belong under advanced features.
- **Why `.mdx`:** it lets the page use `<Callout>` for the desktop-only and Templates-plugin requirements.
- **Cross-links to add:**
  - the "Related" lists in `node-types-templates.md` and `relationship-types.md`;
  - one line in `general-settings.md`, because the export button lives in the General tab;
  - the two commands in `advanced-features/command-palette.md`;
  - one sentence in `sync-and-import.md` saying how this differs from importing nodes (the schema is the structure, not the content).

## Page outline

All UI labels below are the exact strings from the code.

1. **Intro, 2–3 lines.** Share your node types, relation types, relation triples and templates as one `dg-schema-<vault>.json` file, so collaborators start from the same structure. You choose what goes into the export and what to import.
   - **Callout:** desktop only. Templates also need the core **Templates** plugin enabled with a templates folder set.
2. **What's in a schema file.** A short table of the four item types, plus one line on what isn't included: your notes and nodes.
3. **Export a schema:**
   - Open it from **Settings → Discourse Graphs → General → Open export modal**, or run the command **Export discourse graph schema**.
   - Use the selection panel: **Select all** / **Deselect optional**, and the "required by selected triple" rule.
   - Note that only templates used by a node type are checked by default.
   - Finish with **Export schema**, then save the file.
4. **Share the file.** One line: send it however you like (email, chat, a shared drive). This covers the ticket's "share with collaborators" ask.
5. **Import a schema:**
   - Run the command **Import discourse graph schema**, which is only available from the command palette. Then click **Choose schema file**.
   - The preview shows the source vault, the export date, and how many items are new versus already in your vault. Items you already have are tagged "in vault, identical" or "in vault, N field(s) differ".
   - Pick what to import, then click **Import selected**.
6. **When items already exist.** This covers the **Choose what to keep** step:
   - **Keep all mine** and **Use all from <vault>** switch every field of an item at once; each field also has its own choice.
   - Names never change, and why (renaming a type doesn't retag pages already using it).
   - Your template is never overwritten. The imported one is added beside it as `<Name> (from <vault>).md`.
7. **Troubleshooting.** A short list of the real notices:
   - "Schema file is incompatible…" (wrong file or version);
   - template skipped because the Templates plugin isn't set up;
   - a relation skipped because it references a type that isn't in this vault;
   - type names that differ only by case are merged into one.
8. **Related.** Links to node types, relationship types and sync-and-import.

The page should come to about 90–120 lines, which matches the existing feature pages.

## Screenshots and GIFs

I'll capture these over CDP into `public/docs/obsidian/`:

| File | Shows |
|---|---|
| `schema-export-setting.png` | The General tab row with **Open export modal** |
| `schema-export-modal.png` | The selection panel, with one disabled "required by selected triple" box visible |
| `schema-export.gif` | Opening the modal, deselecting an item, then **Export schema** |
| `schema-import-command.png` | Both commands in the command palette |
| `schema-import-preview.png` | The preview: metadata, new/existing counts and the "differ" tags |
| `schema-import-conflicts.png` | **Choose what to keep** with the field table and colour swatches |
| `schema-import.gif` | The full import: choose a file, preview, resolve conflicts, then the success notice |

## Verification

- I'll run the website dev server and check that the page renders, the sidebar entry and every link work, and no image is broken.
- I'll compare each UI string on the page with the code once more after drafting.

One script, `~/.claude/skills/obsidian-vault/scripts/vault.mjs`, owns which worktree builds into which vault. Pass `--worktree <abs path>` on every call: the Bash cwd resets to the main repo between calls.

node $V release --worktree <wt>         # stop this worktree's watcher, free its vault

## The worktree's `.env` follows the lease

The lease is the source of truth, and `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env` mirrors it. Every claim writes `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` and `SUPABASE_USE_DB` there and keeps the other lines. A plain `pnpm dev`, `vault.mjs dev` and `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` therefore all build into the same vault.

- A takeover clears the losing worktree's two keys, but only if they still point at that vault, so its next `pnpm dev` doesn't mirror anywhere.
- `release` clears them the same way.
- Don't hand-edit these keys. Claim or `--take` instead, or the `.env` and the registry disagree.
- A running watcher read `.env` at startup. If `claim` prints `restartWatcher`, restart `pnpm dev`.

- **free**: no lease, nothing running. `claim` takes it silently.
- **idle**: leased to a worktree, but no watcher or CDP run. The session may still be alive and planning.
- **live**: an apps/obsidian `dev.ts` watcher mirrors into it (leased or not, found via `ps` + `lsof` cwd), or a `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` run holds its lock.

A worktree re-claiming gets its own vault back. A lease frees itself only when its worktree directory is gone, or on `release`.

# Obsidian CDP verify

## The one command

From the worktree root:

```sh
node ~/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify/scripts/run.mjs \
  --marker "<string only this change's bundle contains>" \
  --scenario path/to/scenarios.mjs [--scenario more.mjs] [--port 9222] [--skip-build]
```

It runs claim → doctor → launch → deliver → scenarios → cleanup and prints the `last-run.json` path, the scenario matrix, and the `pr-evidence` args. Exit codes: 0 all pass, 1 failure, 2 no vault available or vault locked, 3 marker missing.

On exit 2 with `candidates`, follow the `obsidian-vault` skill: ask Trang which vault to take, then run `vault.mjs claim --take` and rerun.

Write scenario files in the session scratchpad, not the repo.

## Launch

- With no `--slot`, the vault is this worktree's `obsidian-vault` lease. `run.mjs` claims a free one if the worktree has no lease yet. This keeps the CDP run in the vault the worktree's watcher builds into.
- `--slot N` is a legacy override. It's a 1-based index into `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env` and bypasses leases, so use it only when Trang names a slot.
- If Obsidian is running on the debug port, the script attaches.
- If it's running without the port, the script quits Obsidian and relaunches it with `--remote-debugging-port`. Trang approved this; the windows come back.
- If it isn't running, the script launches it with the port.
- It then opens the slot vault through `obsidian://open?path=` and waits for a page target where `.workspace` exists and `app.vault.adapter.basePath` matches the vault.
- It writes the lock `<vault>/.obsidian/dg-verify.lock` (`{pid, branch, startedAt}`) and releases it in `finally`.

## Doctor

`scripts/doctor.mjs [--slot N]` is read-only and prints JSON: the resolved vault, the lock and the Obsidian state. It exits 2 if the worktree has no lease, or if another live run holds the lock. A lock left by a dead pid is ignored.

## Deliver

`scripts/deliver.mjs --marker <str>` also runs on its own.

1. `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH=<slot plugin dir> tsx scripts/build.ts` runs once in `apps/obsidian`. It also writes `apps/obsidian/dist`, which is gitignored.
2. It greps the vault's `main.js` for `--marker` and fails if the marker is absent.
3. It reloads the plugin. The plugin id and folder are resolved from the manifests.
4. It greps again.
5. It warns about other worktrees' apps/obsidian `dev.ts` watchers that mirror into this vault. Your own worktree's watcher builds the same code, so it isn't flagged.

The harness also hashes `main.js` before and after the scenarios. If it changed, the run is marked invalid.

## Drive: scenario contract

A module's `export default` is one scenario or an array of them:

```js
export default {
  name: "Search modal renders",                 // matrix row + screenshot name
  input: "run open-node-search",                // matrix text
  expected: "modal with a textbox and footer",  // matrix text
  setup: async (ctx) => ({ /* state; snapshot anything you change */ }),  // optional
  run: async ({ client, json, vault }, state) => {
    await client.evaluate(`return app.commands.executeCommandById(${json(`${vault.pluginId}:open-node-search`)});`);
    await client.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector(".dg-node-search-modal [role=textbox]")`);
    return client.evaluate(`document.querySelectorAll(".dg-search-footer-action").length`);
  },
  expect: (actual, state) => ({ pass: actual > 0, actual: `${actual} footer actions` }),  // or a boolean
  teardown: async (ctx, state) => {},           // optional: restore what setup changed
};
```

- `ctx` has `client`, `vault` (`root`, `pluginId`, `pluginDir`), `branch`, `json`, `verifyPath(name)` and `writeNote(name, body)`. `writeNote` creates or overwrites `_verify/<branch>/<name>` and returns its path.
- `client` has `evaluate`, `waitFor`, `key`, `typeText`, `pressEscape`, `screenshot`, `reloadPlugin`, `clearModals` and `send` (raw CDP).
- The harness does these for you:
  - Before each scenario, it clears modals and restores the layout captured at the start of the run.
  - After `run`, it takes a screenshot.
  - A thrown error becomes a failing row.
- The worked example is `examples/insert-link-at-cursor.mjs` (ENG-2114, 3 scenarios).

## Evidence

- The artifacts go to `<worktree>/local/obsidian-cdp/artifacts/<branch>/<runStamp>/`: `<n>-<slug>.png` and `last-run.json` (`results[]` of `{scenario, input, expected, actual, pass, screenshot}`).
- Paste the printed matrix into create-pr's Evidence section.
- Upload the screenshots with pr-evidence, using the printed args:

```sh
./apps/roam/node_modules/.bin/tsx ~/.claude/skills/pr-evidence/upload.ts --harness obsidian-cdp <printed args>
```

## Cleanup

- Cleanup dismisses modals (Escape, then force-removes leftover `.modal-container`), restores the baseline layout and releases the lock.
- **It never deletes folders or notes.** `_verify/<branch>/` persists, and reruns overwrite its notes.
- Scenarios that change vault or app settings must restore them in `teardown`.

## Gotchas

These are the ones the code can't handle for you.

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
| --- | --- |
| Double-handled keypress | Pass `type` to `client.key` only through its loop. Never send your own `keyDown`. |
| `editor.hasFocus()` false while focus looks right | This can't be measured over CDP. Assert the consequence instead, e.g. the cursor moved past the inserted text. |
| File content assertion fails, editor looks right | Saves are debounced (about 2s). `waitFor` on `app.vault.read(...)`, and don't read once. |
| `getLeaf(true)` throws "No tab group found" | Every markdown leaf was detached. Use `getLeaf("tab")`. |
| Top-level `await` throws in `evaluate` | Bodies run in a plain function. Return an async IIFE or a promise chain. |
| `iterateRootLeaves` count caps at 2 | A truthy callback return stops the iteration. Use a block body `{ n++; }`. |
| Escape handler in a modal child never wins | Obsidian's modal scope runs first. Push a `Scope` with `app.keymap.pushScope`. |
| Styling CodeMirror spans disappears on focus or scroll | Use a CM6 decoration, not MutationObserver stamping. A widget's `ignoreEvent()` must stay `true` for clicks. |
| Selectors from an old ENG example don't match | The UI drifts. The node search input is now a contenteditable `[role=textbox]`, not an `<input>`. |
| Flaky failure that looks like a code bug | Trang may be using the app mid-run. Rerun before believing a single observation. |
| Timers stall, writes land minutes late | Focus emulation normally prevents this. If it recurs, check `document.visibilityState` and ask Trang to show the window. |
| zsh eats `${VAR}` in `node -e` | Write scenarios to `.mjs` files. |
| `waitFor` on an IIFE always times out | `evaluate` adds an outer `return` only when the code contains no `return`. An IIFE with an inner `return` evaluates to `undefined`, so write `return (() => { ... })()`. |
| A note written in `setup` is randomly missing from search results | Datacore indexes new files after the metadata cache, and the search loads through Datacore. After `writeNote`, also `waitFor` `dc.query("@page and exists(nodeTypeId)")` to include the path. |

Three contract details in `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`'s scenario API. Getting them wrong fails every
scenario with the *same* error, which reads like a product bug rather than a harness mistake — on
ENG-2228 all five scenarios failed identically at "timeout waiting for text shape in store" when
the real cause was the driver calls.

- **`evaluate(expr)` wraps the body in a plain function and only adds a `return` when the string
  contains no `return` at all** (`driver.mjs`: `/\breturn\b/.test(expression) ? expression : "return (…)"`).
  So a self-invoking `(() => { … return x; })()` matches the regex, is treated as a *body*, and
  silently yields `undefined`. Always write an explicit top-level `return …;`.
- **`waitFor(expr)` resolves only when the expression evaluates to literal `true`.** It returns
  `undefined`, never the value. Use it for the condition, then a separate `evaluate` to read data —
  `await waitFor("return shapes.length > 0;")` then `await evaluate("return shapes[0].id;")`.
- **`key()` takes an options object, not a string.** `client.key("t")` spreads a string into the CDP
  params and does nothing; use
  `client.key({ text: "t", key: "t", code: "KeyT", windowsVirtualKeyCode: 84, nativeVirtualKeyCode: 84 })`.
  `typeText` and `pressEscape` are the string-friendly wrappers.

The Sync and Import feature allows you to synchronize your discourse nodes with the Discourse Graph database and share them with collaborators. Once enabled, you can publish nodes to a shared group space and import nodes published by others.

> **Note:** This feature is currently in **beta**. The sync functionality requires an active connection to the Discourse Graph database.

> **Warning:** When using sync and import:
>
> - Don't edit the things you imported
> - Don't click to create new files (from imported nodes)
> - Don't delete imported node types

## Enabling sync mode

### Step 1: Open settings

Open the Discourse Graph plugin settings:

1. Open **Obsidian settings** (click the gear icon in the bottom-left corner, or press `Cmd/Ctrl + ,`)
2. Scroll down in the left sidebar to **community plugins**
3. Find **Discourse Graph**

### Step 2: Reveal the admin panel

The sync feature is located in a hidden **admin panel** tab that is not visible by default.

1. While on the Discourse Graph settings page, press `Cmd + Shift + A` (Mac) or `Ctrl + Shift + A` (Windows/Linux)
2. A new **admin panel** tab will appear in the settings tab bar

![Admin panel tab revealed](/docs/obsidian/sync-setting.png)

### Step 3: Enable sync mode

1. In the **admin panel** tab, find the **(BETA) Sync mode enable** toggle
2. Click the toggle to enable sync mode
3. Click **Save changes**
4. A confirmation notice will appear: "Admin panel settings saved"
5. The sync mode will initialize automatically, and you will see a notice: "Sync mode initialized successfully"

Once enabled, your discourse nodes will begin syncing automatically to the Discourse Graph database. The plugin monitors file changes in your vault (with a short delay) and syncs them in the background.

## Publishing a discourse node

Publishing makes a synced discourse node available to other members of your group. This is how you share your work with collaborators.

### Prerequisites

Before publishing, make sure:

- **Sync mode is enabled** (see above)
- **You are a member of a group.** Group membership is managed by your team administrator. The Discourse Graph team will ensure you are added to the appropriate group before you can publish.
- The discourse node you want to publish has a `nodeTypeId` in its frontmatter
- The discourse node has been **synced at least once** (it must have a `nodeInstanceId` in its frontmatter — this is assigned automatically after the first sync)

import { Callout } from "nextra/components";

Your discourse graph schema is the structure your notes follow: your node types, relation types, the relations allowed between them, and the templates your node types use. Export it to a single JSON file and share it with collaborators, so everyone starts from the same structure. When you import a file, you choose exactly what to bring in and which of your existing settings to keep.

<Callout type="info">
  Schema import and export work in the Obsidian desktop app only. To include
  templates, enable the core **Templates** plugin and set its template folder
  location.
</Callout>

## What a schema file contains

| Item | What is included |
| --- | --- |
| **Node types** | Name, format, template, description, shortcut, color, tag, key image, and folder path |
| **Relation types** | Label, complement, and color |
| **Relation triples** | Which relation types connect which node types (for example, Evidence _supports_ Claim) |
| **Templates** | The full contents of each selected template file |

A schema file never contains your notes or discourse nodes. To share nodes, see [Sync and import](/docs/obsidian/advanced-features/sync-and-import).

## Export your schema

1. Open the export window in either of these ways:
   - Open Obsidian **Settings**, go to **Discourse Graph** > **General**, and click **Open export modal** next to **Export discourse graph schema**
     ![Export discourse graph schema setting](/docs/obsidian/schema-export-setting.png)
   - Open the command palette (`Cmd/Ctrl + P`) and run **Export discourse graph schema**
     ![Schema commands in the command palette](/docs/obsidian/schema-commands.png)
2. Choose what to include. Everything is selected by default, except templates that no node type uses.
   ![Export discourse graph schema window](/docs/obsidian/schema-export-modal.png)
3. Click **Export schema** and choose where to save the file. It is named `dg-schema-<vault name>.json` by default.

![Exporting a schema](/docs/obsidian/schema-export.gif)

### Required items

A selected relation triple needs its node types and its relation type. Those items are marked **required by selected triple** and stay selected. To remove one, first deselect every triple that uses it.

Use **Select all** and **Deselect optional** for node types and relation types, and **Select all** and **Deselect all** for triples and templates.

## Share the file

Send the `.json` file to your collaborators however you like, for example by email, chat, or a shared drive. Anyone with the Discourse Graph plugin can import it into their own vault.

## Import a schema

1. Open the command palette (`Cmd/Ctrl + P`) and run **Import discourse graph schema**
2. Click **Choose schema file** and pick a `dg-schema-*.json` file
3. Review the preview. It shows which vault the file came from, when it was exported, and how many items are new or already in your vault. Items you already have are tagged **in vault, identical** or **in vault, N field(s) differ**.
   ![Import schema preview](/docs/obsidian/schema-import-preview.png)
4. Choose what to import. Everything is selected by default, and the same [required items](#required-items) rule applies.
5. Click **Import selected**. If any selected item differs from what is already in your vault, the button reads **Choose what to keep** instead, and opens the next step.

![Importing a schema](/docs/obsidian/schema-import.gif)

When the import finishes, a notice lists what was created and updated.

## Choose what to keep

When a selected item already exists in your vault with different settings, you decide field by field which value to keep. An item counts as existing when it has the same name, ignoring capitalization.

- Every field starts on your current value, so nothing changes unless you choose it
- Click **Keep all mine** or **Use all from <vault name>** to switch every field of an item at once, or pick each field on its own
- The count at the bottom shows how many fields will come from the file

![Choose what to keep](/docs/obsidian/schema-import-conflicts.png)

An import never renames anything. Renaming a node type would not update the notes that already use it.

### Templates

Importing never overwrites one of your template files. If you choose the file's version of a template you already have, it is added next to yours as `<template name> (from <vault name>).md`, and the node types that use it switch to the new copy.

## Troubleshooting

- **"Schema file is incompatible with this version of the plugin"**: the file is not a schema export, or it came from an incompatible plugin version. Export it again with an up-to-date plugin.
- **Templates are skipped**: enable the core **Templates** plugin and set its template folder location, then export or import again.
- **"Relation … skipped: it references a type that is not in this vault"**: select the node types and relation type that the triple uses, then import again.
- **Two node types become one**: types whose names differ only in capitalization, such as "claim" and "Claim", are treated as the same type.

## Related

- [Configure node types and templates](/docs/obsidian/configuration/node-types-templates)
- [Configure relationship types](/docs/obsidian/configuration/relationship-types)
- [Sync and import nodes](/docs/obsidian/advanced-features/sync-and-import)
